core.text: Every neuter noun in Latin keeps one habit: its object form is the same as its subject form. So **a 3rd-declension neuter noun (corpus, mare: nominative = accusative, plural in -a / -ia)** never takes *-em*: *caput* (head) is both *the head hurts* and *washes the head*. The plural subject and object end in *-a* (*capita*, *corpora*), or in *-ia* for nouns in *-e, -al, -ar* (*maria* seas, *animālia* animals). Latin name: dēclīnātiō tertia, genus neutrum.
Neuter means 'neither masculine nor feminine' — a grammar label, not a fact about the thing. English has no such endings.
Neuter: nominative = accusative; plural in -a; the -e / -al / -ar group adds i (-ia, -ium, ablative -ī).

invented.en: The shepherd sees an animal in the river.

core.text: A masculine or feminine 3rd-declension noun changes for the object — *pāstor → pāstōrem* — and its plural ends in *-ēs*. A neuter one does not change (*caput → caput*) and its plural ends in *-a*. So a bare *corpus* can be the object: *Mārcus corpus lavat* — Marcus washes his body. Check the verb before calling it the subject.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Every neuter noun in Latin keeps one habit, and **a 3rd-declension neuter noun (corpus, mare: nominative = accusative, plural in -a / -ia)** keeps it too: the word it uses as the subject is the very same word it uses as the object. *Corpus* is 'the body' whether the body is doing something or having something done to it. So you cannot tell subject from object by the ending — you read the rest of the sentence.

check.ask: Which word here is the neuter noun — the one that would look the same whether it were the doer or the one done to?

teach.title: The singular: one form for two jobs
teach.say: Look at the table. The nominative (the subject form) and the accusative (the object form) of a neuter noun are one and the same cell: *corpus* is both, and so is *ōs* in the sentences below. There is no *-em* here — *-em* belongs to the masculine and feminine nouns of this family.

show.say: corpus / corpus — the subject cell and the object cell hold the very same word

check.ask: Fill both singular cells of *corpus*. They are one word — write it twice.

teach.title: The plural ends in -a
teach.say: One cell more. The plural subject and object of a neuter noun end in *-a*, hung on the stem you find in the genitive: *corpus, corporis* → *corpora*; *caput, capitis* → *capita*. Again the two cells are the same word.

show.say: corpora / corpora — the plural pair is the same word again, on the genitive's stem

check.ask: Fill both plural cells of *corpus*, using the stem you find in *corporis*.

teach.title: The -e / -al / -ar group keeps an i
teach.say: A small group inside the family — the nouns ending in *-e*, *-al*, *-ar* — keeps an *i* wherever it can. The plural is *-ia*: *mare* → *maria*, *animal* → *animālia*. The genitive plural (the 'of' form) is *-ium*: *marium*. And the ablative singular (the 'by/with/from' form) is *-ī*, not *-e*: *in marī*, in the sea. One extra letter, in three places.

show.say: maria, marium, marī — the i shows in the plural, in the 'of' plural and in the ablative

check.ask: Fill the four cells of *mare* where the extra *i* shows: the two plurals in *-ia*, the genitive plural in *-ium*, and the ablative singular in *-ī*.

teach.title: Telling it from a masculine or feminine one
teach.say: This is the trap. A masculine or feminine 3rd-declension noun does change for the object: *pāstor* → *pāstōrem*, *timor* → *timōrem*. A neuter one does not: *caput* stays *caput*, *cor* stays *cor*. So an unchanged word can still be the object — check the verb before you call it the subject.

check.ask: *sanguinem* and *cor* are both objects of *videt*. Which one shows it in its ending, and which one does not?

teach.title: Using it: let the verb decide
teach.say: Now put it to work. When a neuter noun sits beside a verb, ask who is doing the verb. In *Corpus aegrum medicus bonus sānat* the doer is *medicus* — so *corpus*, though it stands first, is the object.

check.ask: *mel* looks the same as subject and as object. Which is it here, and which word tells you?

more.text: The *-e, -al, -ar* group also has *-ium* in the genitive plural and *-ī* in the ablative singular (*in marī*). The dative and ablative are otherwise the same as for the other 3rd-declension nouns: *capitī, capite; capitibus*. The genitive singular shows the stem — *caput, capitis; corpus, corporis; flūmen, flūminis; ōs, ōris* (mouth); *cor, cordis* (heart) — so learn each noun with its genitive.

The learner's notes (week 11): neuter 3rd-declension nouns behave like the *is*-nouns except in two points — the accusative singular equals the nominative, and the plural nominative and accusative end in *-a* (sometimes *-ia*). Because the nominative can look like anything (*caput, corpus, cor, mel, nōmen, lac*), a form without *-m* can still be an object; only context decides. The *-āre, -ar, -āle, -al* nouns were once 3rd-declension adjectives and keep the adjective's extra *i* (*maria, marium*); watch the ablative *-ī* (*marī*), which is easy to mistake for the dative.

Ørberg's chapter XI list: *flūmen, ōs, crūs* (leg), *corpus, caput, cor, pectus* (chest), *iecur* (liver); *mare, animal*; and *viscera* (organs), plural only. A&G: the *-e, -al, -ar* nouns are i-stems, which is why they take *-ium* and *-ī*; poetry sometimes shows *mare* as an ablative, but the pattern above holds in prose.
